subject: africanElephant
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: adult African bush elephant.
Style: low-poly.
reasoning:
I'm planning the proportions and skeleton structure for an African bush elephant model—working out realistic dimensions and joint placements starting with the hips and spine chain, all facing forward along the Z-axis.

Spine chain runs from hips through three points up to chest, using three named joints (spine1-spine3) parented to hips, with the hips serving as the root spine joint.

For the body surface, I'm thinking about a loft sweep driven by stations along z, skinned to the spine bone chain, but the issue is coverage behind the hips (z<-1.0) where the chain doesn't extend. I'm wondering whether to include hips in the bone list or reposition the root joint toward the rear so the whole body length gets owned by a joint.

Now I'm moving on to the legs, which use a simple limb function with root, target, lengths, and bend direction, starting with the front shoulder position roughly at [±0.55, 2.0, 0.85].

I'll build each leg as a two-segment chain with a slight forward bend at the knee/elbow, attaching front legs to the shoulder joints and hind legs to the hips, naming the joints shoulder/elbow/wrist (or hip/knee/ankle) so the tip lands correctly.

Now I'm sweeping each leg chain into a tapered tube with radii narrowing from thigh to ankle, positioning them at x=±0.6 so they sit just inside the body's width, and shading them with the elephant skin gradient for consistency.

For the skin paint itself, I'm defining base gray tones and building a procedural material with horizontal wrinkle creases driven by noise, darker mottling, and muddy brown tinting near the feet, lightening toward the top of the body.

Refining wrinkle thresholds...

Checking texel density across the body, legs, and ears, and bumping the paint sheet to 2048 to keep wrinkle detail crisp without overloading the atlas. Now thinking about the head shape itself — a domed forehead and cheeks, jointed at the neck.

Since elephants have essentially no neck, I'm sketching a short two-joint neck chain running from the spine's end up to the head base, parented off the last spine joint, then placing the head joint at the top of that chain aimed slightly downward into the face.

For the head itself, I'm positioning the skull as a scaled, flat-shaded low-poly sphere centered around [0, 2.85, 2.05], sized roughly 0.5 wide and 0.6 tall to match elephant proportions.

Now I'm thinking through the trunk, defining it as a catmull-rom chain of points curving down and forward from the forehead base, giving it a natural droop from near the face down toward the ground.

Setting the trunk base just inside the skull front, with the joint chain using a Catmull spline across the points, giving five named joints like trunk1 through trunk5 using a "tentacle" role. I'm defining the sweep radius function to shape the trunk with elliptical cross-sections and ring ridges along its length.

I'm figuring out how to finish the trunk tip — adding small spike fingers at the end plus a nostril detail, maybe darker disc shapes or tiny spheres placed where the trunk's tangent curves forward and down.

For the nostril disc I'm adding two small dark spheres as nostril holes, with the tip radius slightly larger than the disc. For the tusks, I'm shaping ivory cones that curve forward and up from the upper lip base, sweeping down-forward-outward before curling upward like real tusks.

Still refining tusk curve points...

Now I'm shaping the ears as a large extruded outline attached at the head, sized roughly 1.4m tall and 1.2m wide to mimic the big Africa-shaped silhouette, with the outline directions set so it projects outward from the skull.

Mapping out the ear outline points now, tracing a rounded top that tapers into a sharp pointed bottom, with the attachment edge running vertically at the base.

Now I'm figuring out the ear's orientation on the head, positioning it behind the eye with an outward-and-back angle so it drapes naturally over the shoulder area, mirroring left and right using the sign direction.

I want to differentiate the inner ear with a pinkish tone versus a darker outer rim, figuring out which face normal corresponds to the outward-facing side so I can paint accordingly, then mirroring that logic for the opposite ear.

Since calculating the exact rim distance is tricky, I'll simplify by skipping fine inner/outer differentiation and instead just giving the ears a pink-gray tone, darkening the side walls where the extrude bevel creates them using the normal's thickness component.

I'm also considering whether to add vein-like texture to the ears via a small textured plane overlay positioned on the ear's outer face, aligned to the ear's local orientation, though this adds complexity given the part's frame and quaternion setup.

Right now the texture ends up on the inner face for one ear and outer for the other, so it's asymmetric. The simplest fix is just placing a decal plane on both faces (+z and -z) so each ear gets veins visible from the outside regardless of orientation sign.

To avoid the plane sticking out past the ear's silhouette, I need to clip the vein texture to the ear outline shape, so I'll generate an SVG whose clip path matches the ear's own contour coordinates before drawing the veins and wrinkle strokes inside it.

I realize rotating the back plane 180° about local Y will flip the texture's u-direction relative to the ear outline, causing a mirrored mismatch between the texture and the shape on that side.

I need to figure out the texture mirroring so that after rotating the back plane 180°, the ear root lines up correctly on the viewer's side, which means creating a mirrored SVG with a flipped transform so u=0 ends up on the correct edge.

Actually, this is getting too convoluted -- a simpler approach might be to skip the back face entirely and instead paint the veins directly onto the ear extrude using a procedural function based on position: radiating lines from the root computed via angle and noise, plus some patches, driven by a coordinate-based paint.

Making earPaint a function of thick so both ears share the same logic, then considering adding a proper ear joint under the head for rigging, with its direction angled outward and down to match the ear's flap-like hinge motion.

For the eyes, I'm planning to place small decals on the skull surface using surface hit coordinates (azimuth and elevation) so they sit naturally on the head, with a simple amber iris texture including a highlight and lid wrinkle lines, using the hit normal to orient the decal direction automatically.

Now I'm moving to overall head construction: the skull sphere plus cheek, temple, forehead bump, and brow ridges, with a separate jaw part parented to the head. I'm sketching the jaw as a flattened, scaled sphere positioned below the trunk base to form the mouth, with a pink-gray interior color and its own joint angled forward-down.

I'm checking the head silhouette against the body — comparing skull radius and center position to shoulder height, and adjusting the skull's vertical placement slightly lower so the head doesn't sit too far above the shoulders, aiming for realistic elephant proportions.

Now I'm adding twin forehead domes for that characteristic bulge, then placing cheek spheres and a brow ridge, plus considering a small dark temporal gland streak below the eye for added realism.

For the body, I'm defining a series of cross-section stations along the spine, each with a center position, width, and height, working from the rump through the hips to the belly to shape the torso's overall silhouette like a real elephant's low-slung belly.

I'm continuing to plot stations along the body toward the shoulder and neck, tapering width and height while shifting the center height to shape the back dip and shoulder rise, then narrowing further to blend into the head.

For the loft's cross-section, I'm deciding on a faceted low-poly look with around 10 sides and flat shading rather than smooth, to keep that chunky style consistent across the deformed sections.

I'm checking that the chest-to-neck-to-head transition overlaps properly in height, then thinking through the elephant's characteristic saddle-back dip behind the shoulders and raised hip area, adjusting the loft's vertical profile at the shoulder and hip z-positions to capture that silhouette.

Now I'm working out the leg geometry—placing the limb root near the shoulder and the target near the ankle, calculating the distance between them so the two-segment leg chain (upper and lower leg lengths) bends correctly to reach the foot, which I'll model as a short cylinder sitting at ground level.

Adding a dark foot pad ring near the sole, then moving to leg sweeps for smooth skin along the bone chain, and setting up hind leg roots, targets, lengths, and bend directions.

Now I'm working out the limb joint arrays as polylines fed into the chain-sweep function, confirming corner rounding handles the bends smoothly. Then I'm designing the tail as a thin tapering chain from the rump down to a tuft, defining catmull points for tail1 through tail3 segments.

For the tuft I'm planning a spiky bristle ring around the tail tip — using a ring of spike elements angled outward and tilted to droop along the tail's downward direction.

I'm checking that ChainPoint frames convert properly to lines for the spike placement, confirming hips as the root joint with the spine chain starting at the same position, and verifying the tail bone chain sweeps correctly from inside the rump. I'm also planning extra skin-wrinkle rings along the trunk sweep.

For the trunk's bolder ridge look, I'm designing a skin paint function parameterized by a ridge pattern based on surface position and coordinates, deciding to support both height-based and tangent-based wrinkle modes, and working out the typing for the paint function using Vector3 and SurfaceCoords types.

I'm also planning finer details: small toenails, a lip collar skipped for simplicity, a jawline, and dust/mud effects -- reddish-brown African soil tones on the lower legs and a lighter tan dust coating on the back from dust-bathing behavior.

Adding sparse head hair and forehead bristle tufts...

Now tallying up the full part count: body, four leg sweeps with feet, pads, and toenails, the tail with bristles, trunk and nostril, tusks, ears, and skull details — making sure everything adds up before moving forward.

I'm realizing I need more density to hit the target range, so I'm planning to add wrinkle rings along the trunk using small torus shapes oriented along the sweep's tangent at each segment, plus skin fold creases and tusk ring details to flesh out the texture and part count further.

I'm matching the torus radius to the same radius function used elsewhere in the sweep, using the chain point's t value so the ridge rings track the trunk's taper consistently. Since anything placed on a point inherits that point's bones, the torus rides rigidly rather than deforming smoothly, so I'm considering an alternative ridge approach that matches the taper more precisely.

I'm planning similar ring details for the legs, maybe adding ankle skin fold rings using three torus rings positioned on the lower leg chain, plus considering body wrinkle lines like a belly crease or shoulder fold as decal textures rather than geometry.

I'm settling on using decals for these surface details instead of geometry: shoulder/hip crease arcs, cheek/trunk base wrinkles, a mud splash on the flanks, and vein painting on the ears, alongside the eye texture, applying them to the body sweep surface at specific hit points.

Writing SVG texture code...

For mud, I'm adding irregular brown blobs and small splatter circles as a decal on the belly and lower flanks of the body.

For the skull, I'm placing cheek fold lines near the mouth, then positioning the eye at a sideways-biased azimuth to match an elephant's lateral eye placement, using the skull's center point as the reference for orientation. I'll size the eye to match a 100x64 texture aspect ratio before drawing it.

The eye itself gets an almond shape with dark skin-toned lids and an amber iris, scaled small relative to the skull. Since elephant eyes sit on the sides of the head rather than the front, I'm deciding this is fine even though they'll be only partially visible from a front view.

For the overall skin, I want a single continuous paint function shared across body, legs, head, and trunk so the noise field reads as one organism rather than disjointed parts. I'm building this skin paint by layering large-scale gray blotching, fine-grained darker noise, crease highlighting along ridges, and a dusty tan overlay on top.

I'm adding reddish soil staining near the ground, underside shading from ambient occlusion, and defining separate ridge functions for body, legs, and trunk so wrinkle frequency and orientation differ per body part while still using the same base paint logic.

With 18 tori positioned at (i+0.5)/18 along the trunk, I want the dark crease paint to fall between torus centers, so I'm setting the crease value using a cosine at 18 periods so it peaks exactly at the gaps between tori.

Now I'm working out how the sweep parameter t maps to arc length along the chain, and planning the trunk layout: reserving the first 0.1 of t for the head region, placing torus rings from 0.1 onward, and defining a leg radius function that interpolates across a small array of radii for the wrinkle rings on the lower legs around t=0.6 to 0.9.

I'm writing a shared keyed interpolation helper so the sweep radius function and the torus ring radii stay consistent, then checking how the leg chain terminates at the ankle and how the foot cylinder and end cap geometry overlap there to avoid gaps.

For the foot bone I'm referencing the leg chain's tip joint (the wrist/ankle) rather than a separate bone, and planning toenail placement as small boxes arranged around the front of the foot at a few angular offsets.

Positioning nails...

Adjusting nail color to a darker tan, keeping foot cylinders capped and flat-shaded. I'm also sketching the trunk tip details — eye, brows, temporal gland — and considering whether a small finger-like cone on the dorsal trunk tip would read well, deciding instead to keep a flat cut with a nostril disc angled down-forward along the trunk's final segment direction.

Now I'm laying out the actual trunk curve points, seven in total forming six spans (T0 through T6), curving the trunk forward and gently upward toward the tip using centripetal Catmull-Rom smoothing, and tapering its radius from about 0.33 near the base down toward 0.13 near the tip so it hovers just above the ground.

I'm also figuring out the trunk's blend with the forehead -- widening the root to around 0.36-0.4 so it merges naturally into the skull -- and working out where the tusks should emerge near the lip beside the trunk, calculating the skull's narrowing ellipsoid profile at that height to place the tusk start point correctly.

I'm checking that the body, neck, and skull segments overlap enough to avoid visible gaps in the rigging, adding a bulking "face" shape near the forehead to broaden the front and anchor the tusks inside that mass.

Now I'm positioning the ears relative to the head: computing their origin, direction, and span to see whether they end up rising above the skull's top, which seems too tall, so I'm adjusting the vertical placement slightly lower to keep proportions believable.

For orientation, I'm checking the attachment point against the skull surface at that location to confirm it lines up, and I'm deciding to keep the ear's angle vector simple rather than adding extra outward flare for now.

I'm setting up the ear joint with its direction vector, keeping the extrude flat since low-poly ears don't need much curl, maybe just a thickened rim sweep for detail.

Skipping extra fold geometry for now, I'm shifting to the body structure: hips as the root joint, with hind legs parented to hips and front legs to spine3, then building a spine chain via catmull points with named segments spine1-3 under hips. For the body loft, I need stations of position/width/height along that spine chain to drive the mesh shape.

For the loft stations, I'm deciding to skip including hips as a bone since it would create a zero-length segment where hips meets spine1 at the same position, so I'll loft only along the spine chain itself, letting the rearmost stations clamp to spine1 since they fall before the chain's start. I'm also considering whether a separate neck sweep is needed, but since the body loft already overlaps into the skull/chest region, it may be redundant.

Now I'm sketching out the neck and head joints — placing neck1, neck2 along a short upward path, then adding a thick skin tube around the neck for cheap coverage, followed by a head joint at the neck's end and a jaw joint aimed forward from it, noting the jaw doesn't need a child joint since it has no further bone chain.

For the jaw itself I'm adding a flattened sphere for the lower jaw mesh, skipping the mouth interior for simplicity, and considering a slightly lighter lower lip shape, acknowledging the chin will mostly be hidden from the front but visible from the side. I'm also keeping the skull faceted with low-poly flat shading, treating the tusks as rigid attachments to the head without their own joint, and adding a small gray ring at the tusk base to suggest a sheath, while deciding to skip eyelashes, mud, and ground details and move on to the tail.

Now I'm padding out the remaining detail list to boost part count and realism: toe nails, wrinkle rings along the trunk and ankles, a darker belly stripe, forehead hair spikes, chin whiskers and base bristles, a lighter inner-ear patch, tail tuft spikes, temple gland streaks, eyebrow ridge capsules, and cheek bulges.

I'm also deciding against overly fussy details like ear notches or rim stiffeners to keep things simple, while adding forehead domes and considering spine bristles but skipping them for accuracy reasons, and instead planning small sphere lumps at the knee and elbow joints positioned slightly forward to suggest bone structure on both front and hind legs.

I'm adding muscular shoulder and hip bulges using scaled spheres positioned on the spine and hip bones to build a heavier silhouette, plus a subtle pink-gray tint on the belly underside using a smoothstep blend based on surface normal. I'm deciding no background rock or glow is needed, and considering whether to add a mouth line decal beneath the trunk to suggest the mouth curve.

Now I'm placing facial crease decals on the skull, combining mouth lines and wrinkles into a face-folds texture positioned near the lower front of the skull, with eye wrinkle rays as a separate decal. I'm tallying up the texture set -- eye, shoulder folds, hip folds, face folds, and mud -- landing on five total, which feels sufficient.

Starting the actual implementation now, importing the builder utilities (frame, rng, aim, limb, paint, noise, smoothstep, svg, etc.) needed to construct the model.

Writing skin color palette and paint functions...

Checking type inference for the array literal...

Actually to be safer, I'll avoid the array return and instead blend colors with a mix function toward a dark shade based on normal, which sidesteps the tuple typing issue entirely. Now I'm thinking about the ridge paint function on the body, where surface coordinates come through as `[t, deg]` typed as SurfaceCoords from the callback.

Defining ridge functions for body, legs, trunk, and head, each using sine or cosine waves with different frequencies combined with smoothstep to create thin crest lines, plus noise warping for texture variation. I also need to plan out separate paint objects per variant, with a shared skin paint helper taking the ridge function.

Writing ear paint shader...

Checking the ear normal logic for the thickness comparison, confirming the color input resolves fine, and verifying the bevel and extrude vectors stay normalized through the mesh generation.

Now I'm weighing whether to import the OutlinePoint type directly from the builder module versus inlining the outline array literal in the call to let TypeScript infer the shape contextually, since the type export path is uncertain.

I'm tracing through the point sequence to verify the outline doesn't self-intersect, checking the path from the top curve down through the sharp point and back to the base.

Marking the tip vertex sharp and keeping the smoothing level low so corner-cutting doesn't risk crossing adjacent edges. For the loft call itself, I'm unsure whether the options support a "sides" parameter, so I'll leave it out and rely on the default behavior.

For body geometry I'm settling on 10-sided faceted lofts with smooth disabled, giving a low-poly octagonal/decagonal barrel look, and legs get an 8-sided sweep with the same faceted, non-smoothed style.

For the limb construction I'm planning a helper function that takes a root point, foot target, segment lengths, and bend directions, passing a single bend vector like [[0,0,1]] to keep the knee angle simple, while sidestepping explicit Joint typing by inferring parent types from the builder's own return values.

Now I'm working out the leg builder itself, which generates chain points via the limb helper and wires them into a named chain with proper parent joints -- keeping front and hind leg joint names distinct (shoulder/elbow/wrist vs hip/knee/ankle) with left/right suffixes so each chain gets a unique identifier.

I'm defining the sweep radius function for leg thickness, then adding foot parts as cylinder geometry attached to the wrist/ankle bone, positioned at the foot target location.

Adding toenail details...

Adding wrinkle rings along the leg chains using torus geometry...

Working out torus placement around the leg's octagonal cross-section so the ring sits just outside the flats without clipping, adjusting the radius and tube thickness slightly to account for the polygon's vertex-to-flat difference.

Setting end caps round at the start and flat at the tip, then placing a small dark nostril disc at the trunk's endpoint using its tangent direction for orientation, inheriting bone transform from the last trunk joint.

Adding nostril holes as tiny spheres offset laterally using the binormal direction, pushed slightly forward along the tangent for depth. I'm deciding to skip the lower trunk finger detail for now and move on to scattering hair spikes across the skull surface.

For the hair, I'm scattering small flat-colored cones over the top of the skull filtered by normal direction and height, embedding them partway into the surface. Since the forehead domes sit near the top of the skull and could clash with the hair placement, I'm considering scattering across the skull plus both dome surfaces together with a filter restricting to upward-facing points above a certain height, making sure hairs don't spawn where they'd be hidden inside the domes.

I'm skipping chin, cheek, and whisker details, but adding sparse coarse body hair stubble on the back using a small scatter of dark-brown spikes filtered to upward-facing surfaces.

Now I'm moving to decals — folds on the shoulders, hips, face, and eyes using a decal API that projects a texture onto a target mesh at a given position and direction. Writing SVG code...

For the fold textures, I'm scaling stroke widths appropriately for a 256px decal size and considering a lighter color for subtlety, then planning two distinct fold textures — concentric arcs for shoulders and vertical creases for hips — with mirrored decals on the left and right sides of the body.

Working out the orientation math for how the decal's local axes map onto the viewer's perspective when looking at the model's left versus right side, so the mirroring stays consistent rather than reversed. Now I'm thinking through a mud splash texture using irregular blot shapes.

Adding dark belly spots and face fold decals, figuring out placement coordinates on the body's lower curve, then starting an SVG for an eye shape with an almond outline.

Calculating the curve's vertical bounds, the almond top sits near y=14 and bottom near y=52, so I'm shrinking the iris radius slightly to ry 17 to keep it contained, then clipping it with clipPath.

For placing eye decals on the skull, I'm computing hit positions via a surface raycast around a center point with mirrored azimuth for left/right sides, and need to guard against null hits by skipping those. I'm also checking whether the cheek geometry might occlude the eye position given their relative heights, since the surface-around query returns the outermost hit from any mesh in that direction.

I'm adding a brow ridge above each eye using a capsule shape, positioning its endpoints roughly above the computed eye location based on the ellipsoid's azimuth/elevation math.

Now I'm placing a small dark temple gland streak behind the eye, computing its surface position from the skull ellipsoid equations and giving it a thin dark-colored ellipsoid shape.

I'm checking overall proportions next—total body length around 6.4m from tusk tip to tail, standing height near 3.8m at the ears, with feet resting at y=0 so the model sits flush on the ground plane.

Now I'm adding shoulder and hip bulges using scaled spheres positioned along the spine and hip bones, sized so they poke slightly beyond the body's silhouette for a natural muscular look, then starting on the tusk's banding detail.

Defining tusk shape...

Trimming the curve slightly shorter to around 2.4m keeps it realistic while leaving 1.8m exposed, which works fine. Checking the trunk and tusk clearance confirms the geometry doesn't overlap, and I'm now sizing the tail tuft and setting up the tail chain sweep with tapered radii.

Working out the tail color (skin near the rump, dark bristle tuft) and the neck sweep geometry, making sure the rounded cap at the neck's start stays hidden inside the body and that the spine chain connects cleanly to the neck's starting point. Now defining the paint objects for different body regions—skin for body, legs, head, trunk—plus a plain paint variant for lumps, feet, and jaw.

Checking the texel density across all painted surfaces: adding up body, legs, trunk, head, and ear areas to roughly 75 square meters, then calculating that a 2048 sheet gives about 5mm per texel, which is fine for the 1-1.5cm creases I need.

Now I'm counting flat colors like ivory, tusk base, nail, pad, bristle, nostril, and jaw interior—about 12 total—and confirming the atlas fits painted textures plus flat colors into a 4096 sheet. I'm also planning a small pink ellipsoid for the mouth interior, positioned between the upper face and jaw under the trunk root.

Setting up the module imports and metadata for the elephant model builder.

Building out the elephant's skeleton now, defining joints and spine chain with coordinate positions...

Still defining jaw joint, then building the trunk chain with six segments matching the catmull spline points, checking that span counts align with names and considering centripetal parameterization.

Setting up the tail chain rooted inside the rump mesh, verifying its endpoints stay within the body silhouette and clear the floor, then moving to leg geometry where I'm checking root and foot positions give a moderate knee bend given the limb segment lengths versus the straight-line distance.

That knee offset of about 0.2 forward is fine. For the front legs I'm figuring out bend direction—elbow bends backward while the carpus bends forward, so I need to pick a hint vector that makes the joint arc the right way without the wrist ending up behind the leg line.

Settling on front legs bending backward at the elbow and hind legs bending forward, keeping the elephant's legs nearly straight with just a subtle forward angle at the carpus. I'm also keying the leg radii so the thigh tapers down the limb while staying tucked inside the body width, and working out the joint chain positions starting from the shoulder joint relative to the spine root.

Now writing the leg-building function that constructs front and hind limb chains with their own root/foot positions, bend directions, and joint names...

Checking the rear leg root's parent position relative to hips, confirming joint positions are consistent with the x>0 convention for the left side across the chain.

I'm working through adding ring geometry along the leg chain using torus shapes, and double-checking how the `at` parameter type resolves for frame/direction inputs in the part options.

Next I'm positioning a knee lump as a small sphere offset forward or backward from the joint depending on whether it's a front or hind leg, scaling it to look like a joint bulge.

Writing body loft profile...

Checking the remaining z-stations, the belly and top stay consistent through the back half. I'm a bit concerned the narrow 0.45 radius at the rear station makes the tail end look pointy, and the loft's default rounded cap might push the rump further out than intended, around z -2.4 or so.

I'm tweaking the rear stations to control exactly where the elephant's rump ends and how rounded it looks. Testing flat vs round caps, and adjusting the final station's width and height so the dome doesn't extend too far past -2.0, keeping the silhouette looking like a proper rounded hindquarters rather than an odd bulge near -2.6.

Given that uncertainty, I'm setting the tail's root points to begin tucked inside the body (around z=-2.0 to -2.45) so it emerges naturally from the rump surface once the dome geometry is sorted out, with the tail curving down and back along y and z coordinates toward the tip.

Since real tail roots sit about a meter behind the hind legs, I'm nudging the last station to z=-1.65, putting the back around -2.35 and giving roughly 1.25m clearance from the rear leg—adjusting the tail points by +0.15 in z accordingly.

I'm finalizing seven body cross-section stations spanning from the tail base around z=-1.65 up through the shoulders and into the head region near z=1.85, each with its own width, height, and y-position to shape the silhouette via a Catmull spline, then adding shoulder fold decals on the body surface.

Now I'm figuring out where the hip and mud decals land, and whether the decals should target just the body surface or also the bulge spheres sitting on top of it, since the shoulder bulge sticks out past the body and could hide the decal underneath.

I decide to dial back how pronounced the bulges are so they don't overshadow the decals, and just target both body and bulge regardless of overlap. Now I'm moving on to defining the head parts, starting with the skull sphere's position and scale.

Adding domes, face bulk, cheeks...

Working out eye and face-fold decal placement, confirming the azimuth convention where left side is positive, and making sure eyes hit the skull directly rather than through the ear. Now setting up body stubble scatter with distance and filter constraints.

Adding trunk ring geometry...

Working out the crease boundary formula...

I'm setting the segment step between 0.14 and 0.97 across 16 divisions, and defining a trunk radius function that tapers from 0.36 down to 0.1 along keyed positions. I'm now computing each ear's placement using vector math for left and right sides symmetrically.

Writing ear extrusion code...

I'll use the options form for color and bone instead. Now adding a bristle ring around the tail end using spikes arranged via b.ring, though I'm unsure if spike supports a sides parameter since it's sweep-based — might be safer to omit it.

I'll simplify to just color for the bristle ring, trusting the tilt to lean bristles along the tail's tangent direction, and add a second larger ring with more bristles and longer length for a fuller tuft look. Then I'm moving to decal texture setup, making sure the texture aspect ratio matches the target size to avoid distortion, before starting on the SVG for the eye.

Writing SVG code...

Still writing SVG code...

Writing SVG shapes for face wrinkles and mud blobs...

I'm checking edge cases like decal projection for vertices without a surface hit, head joint roles, leg contacts, and skull surface assignment—confirming the bone weighting for body decals is handled correctly. I'm also verifying smaller details like trunk sweep sides, cap shapes for the trunk sweep, and neck sweep radius to make sure everything is consistent.

Now I'm writing the jaw geometry using small flattened spheres for the jaw and mouth, parented to the jaw bone, and confirming that the scale option accepts a tuple as seen in other toon examples. I'm checking that the mouth sphere stays mostly hidden inside the jaw shape except for a slight peek, which should look fine, and I'm planning to add a pink inner-ear patch next.

Now I'm reviewing the earlier ear base color, then tuning the foot soil tinting so a reddish-brown dust color blends in strongly near the ground using a smoothstep based on height, giving a convincing dusty African terrain look on the legs. I'm also double-checking that the paint function signature always passes the surface parameter through even when unused by the ridge calculation.

I'm verifying that ridge detailing correctly uses different surface parameters depending on context—trunk uses one component, lofted/swept parts use t and degree, and spherical head parts use UV coordinates—then confirming the bristle, lash, and nerve detailing are all finished. I check that the hinge joint role typing is just a valid string literal, and that leg ordering relative to decals is correct, before moving to verify the nostril offset function usage with the feather direction parameter.

Now I'm working out the trunk tip nostril placement, positioning a cylinder disc at the tip offset slightly forward along the trunk's direction, then adding small dark spheres as nostril detail using the tip's binormal to spread them sideways. I confirm the trunk has six joints with a flat end cap at the tip, and move on to checking the pad cylinder color and sizing before adding a tusk ring cap color.

I'm double-checking the builder's `along` method signature, confirming all imports are actually used (removing an unused `random` import), and verifying that the ear outline typing works correctly with the extrude function's expected parameter shape. I note that ear painting logic lives outside the build function since it only needs THREE, and move on to picking colors for the ear segments.

Now I'm filling in colors for creases, writing the forehead hair filter condition based on normal and position thresholds, and placing the face decal using azimuth and elevation hits within the head skin arrays. I decide against adding a navel detail and move to writing out the full code, estimating it'll run around 450 lines covering tusk and ear naming.
